introduction-the-privacy-leak.core: Even with HTTPS everywhere, traditional DNS queries travel in plaintext over UDP 53, revealing every domain you visit to your ISP, the Wi-Fi operator or anyone on-path, who can also tamper with answers. Encrypted DNS (DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS) closes that leak between client and resolver, though the resolver still sees your queries.

first_principles.problem: A coffee-shop Wi-Fi operator logs and injects ads based on every domain customers look up.
truths: HTTPS hides content, not DNS lookups.
Plaintext can be read and modified.
Encryption needs an endpoint you trust.

analogy.title: Sealing letters but writing addresses on postcards
analogy.story: Your letters are private, but the postcards asking for addresses are readable by every postman.
analogy.breaks: Postcards can't be altered undetectably; DNS answers can.

code.text:
sudo tcpdump -ni wlan0 udp port 53 -l | grep -o 'A? [^ ]*'
# A? bank.example.
# A? health-clinic.example.

check.q: Does HTTPS hide which domains you look up?
check.a: No, standard DNS queries are plaintext, and SNI also reveals the hostname unless ECH is used.

how-traditional-dns-works-the-unencrypte.core: A stub resolver on your device sends a small UDP packet to port 53 of a recursive resolver configured via DHCP. The query has a random ID and source port; the response is accepted if they match. There is no encryption or authentication, so on-path attackers read everything and off-path attackers can attempt cache poisoning by guessing IDs and ports, as in the Kaminsky attack.

first_principles.problem: An engineer assumes DNS answers are trustworthy because they 'come from the resolver'.
truths: Matching uses ID and port only.

analogy.title: Shouting a question across a crowded room
analogy.story: Anyone can hear it, and anyone shouting back with the right ticket number might be believed.
analogy.breaks: Rooms are small; the internet has many on-path observers.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows ID and plaintext UDP transport.

code.text:
dig example.com A +noedns
# ;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 41237
# ;; SERVER: 192.168.1.1#53(UDP)

check.q: What did the Kaminsky attack exploit?
check.a: Weak randomness in DNS query IDs/ports, letting off-path attackers flood forged answers to poison resolver caches.

dns-over-tls-dot-the-dedicated-lane.core: DNS over TLS (RFC 7858) wraps standard DNS messages in a TLS session on TCP port 853. It's simple and standardised and supported by Android's Private DNS, systemd-resolved and Unbound. Because it uses a dedicated port, networks can easily see that DoT is in use, and block it to force plaintext fallback, which is good for enterprise control and bad for censorship resistance.

first_principles.problem: A privacy-focused admin wants OS-wide encrypted DNS without depending on browser settings.

analogy.title: A dedicated armoured van lane
analogy.story: Your messages are locked in an armoured van, but everyone can see the van in its special lane.
analogy.breaks: Armoured vans are rare; port 853 traffic is easy to fingerprint.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: All system lookups encrypted to authenticated resolvers.

check.q: What does strict mode in DoT mean?
check.a: The client refuses to fall back to plaintext if a TLS connection to the authenticated resolver can't be established.

dns-over-https-doh-the-camouflage.core: DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484) sends DNS messages as HTTP requests (application/dns-message) over HTTPS on port 443, blending in with ordinary web traffic. It's hard to block without breaking the web and is built into browsers (Firefox, Chrome) and OSes. The trade-off: it can bypass enterprise DNS controls and split-horizon zones, and it concentrates queries at a few large resolvers.

first_principles.problem: A browser silently switches to a public DoH resolver and internal hostnames stop resolving.
truths: Applications can choose their own resolver.
Enterprise DNS policies assume the OS resolver.

analogy.title: Hiding letters inside ordinary parcels
analogy.story: Your question travels inside normal-looking packages on the main road, impossible to single out.
analogy.breaks: Parcels can be X-rayed; DoH endpoints can still be blocked by IP/hostname lists.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: DNS answer fetched over ordinary HTTPS.

check.q: Why is DoH harder for networks to block than DoT?
check.a: It uses port 443 and looks like ordinary HTTPS, so blocking it risks breaking normal web traffic.

the-privacy-paradox-trading-one-watcher-.core: Encrypted DNS hides queries from the network path, but the resolver still sees all of them. Moving from your ISP's resolver to a big public one trades one watcher for another, and concentrates the internet's DNS data with a few companies. Mitigations include choosing resolvers with audited no-logging policies, Oblivious DoH (a proxy separating who asks from what's asked), and running your own recursive resolver.

first_principles.problem: Users enable DoH thinking they're anonymous, but their resolver logs every query with their IP.
truths: Separating identity from content reduces exposure.

analogy.title: Swapping a nosy neighbour for a nosy concierge
analogy.story: The street can't see your mail anymore, but the concierge who forwards it still can.
analogy.breaks: Concierges can be vetted personally; resolver policies must be trusted.

example.title: Oblivious DoH
flow: Client encrypts query to target resolver's key
Sends via proxy (sees IP, not query)
Target decrypts query (sees query, not IP)

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No single party sees both who and what.

check.a: It separates client identity (seen by the proxy) from query content (seen by the resolver), so neither knows both.

the-enterprise-challenge-split-horizon-d.core: Enterprises rely on internal resolvers for split-horizon zones, security filtering and logging, and browser DoH can bypass all of it. Controls include the canary domain use-application-dns.net (if the network's resolver returns NXDOMAIN for it, Firefox disables default DoH), browser enterprise policies, running an internal DoH/DoT resolver, and blocking known public DoH endpoints at the firewall.

first_principles.problem: After a browser update, employees can't reach intranet sites, and DNS-based malware filtering stops working.
truths: Browsers default to public DoH in some regions.
Signals and policies can steer clients.

analogy.title: A company post room with a 'use internal mail' sign
analogy.story: The sign tells couriers to route through the post room so internal addresses and security checks work.
analogy.breaks: Signs are honoured voluntarily; malware ignores the canary.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Browsers use the corporate encrypted resolver; intranet works.

code.text:
# Internal resolver (Unbound)
local-zone: "use-application-dns.net." always_nxdomain

# Chrome policy (JSON)
{ "DnsOverHttpsMode": "secure",
  "DnsOverHttpsTemplates": "https://doh.corp.example.com/dns-query" }

check.q: What does returning NXDOMAIN for use-application-dns.net do?
check.a: Signals to browsers like Firefox that the network wants them to disable default DoH and use the local resolver.
